doc.title: Stanley Dance interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Ghostwriting Music Is My Mistress and why Ellington trusted him
summary: Dance describes Doubleday's offer to Ellington, working as his ghost, traveling with him, and attending his sessions including Afro-Bossa.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Well I don’t think we needed to have been as careful as we were about that. When it got back to England, some of the performances were edited down because we’d gotten a little more time than we should have had, but I don’t think we needed to have done that. I don’t think the union has time to check all those you know. But the company didn’t want any trouble there. It wasn’t because of the artists. But subsequently I made a lot of records for Dennis Preston’s label in England, English Columbia. And by this time I was getting sort of involved with Ellington, when Doubleday finally agreed with him to do Music is my Mistress, his book. Doubleday was up at the Rainbow Grill and Tope says to Duke, “Well it’s high time we had your book, Mr. Ellington.” And Duke said, “Well how much, Mr. Doubleday?” And he said something, I forget how much it was, but it seemed a lot of money at the time, $50,000 or something like that. And he said, “Well yeah, we’ll do it” he said, “if Stanley will work with me on it.” And so I was the ghost you know, which was very good because it meant that I traveled around with him quite a lot. And my contribution was not really — well it was sort of rephrasing some things, but as far as possible, it was just as he said it you know. But I had to program it.

Because I guess he realized I was harmless. No, but I mean by this time well he knew my wife from way back, and her brother through, they used to play bridge together. And I think you know, I used to go to all his record sessions and everything, and he just got accustomed to my face.
Yeah, well, I thought it might.
You were present during the “Afro-Bossa” recording also?
